children: A coalition of auto industry groups urged President Trump to keep Chinese cars out of the U.S. ahead of a meeting with leader Xi Jinping, saying any entry by Chinese newcomers would undermine jobs and national security.

In advance of Trump's state dinner next week with Jinping, the group-including the Alliance for Automotive Innovation and the National Automobile Dealers Association-implored the president to "maintain policies that keep the door firmly shut to Chinese automakers seeking to sell, import or manufacture vehicles inside the U.S."
"Allowing them to open a domestic facility would provide a foothold in the U.S. market at the expense of manufacturers operating here," the coalition wrote in a letter sent Thursday to Trump.
The letter underscores rising anxiety in the car industry and corporate America that Trump is angling to notch a deal with Xi that would invite more investment in the U.S. by Chinese companies.
Trump told Fox News last week that he opposes Chinese car imports into the U.S., but said he would welcome Chinese automakers building vehicles in America.

"If China wanted to come in, and open a plant to build their cars here, I'd be OK with it. Japan does it-but they hire our people," Trump said. "What I don't want is them to build in Mexico and just, you know, build it inexpensively and ship it across the border."
A White House spokesperson didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Lately, the Trump administration has taken a hardened stance toward imported Chinese vehicles and tie-ups between domestic carmakers and competitors in China.

In June, Trump's Commerce Department banned Polestar, the majority-Chinese-owned electric car brand, from selling cars in the U.S., after both sides failed to reach an agreement that would put the company in compliance with a regulation banning internet-connected Chinese software in new vehicles.

This month, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy lambasted Ford Motor's business dealings with Chinese automotive firms, including a battery plant joint venture with a Chinese firm in Michigan and a factory tie-up in Spain with automaker Geely.
Ford Chief Executive Jim Farley later told The Wall Street Journal that the letter reflected "basic misunderstandings" about its operations.
Congress has also been debating legislation that would stamp out imports of Chinese vehicles and manufacturing.

China's car industry has consumed market share from traditional automakers around the world. Volkswagen's supervisory board this month approved a plan to cut 100,000 jobs and halve its model portfolio, in part due to the strain of increasing competition.

Chinese car companies have avoided expanding to the U.S. by and large because of the software ban and tariffs in excess of 100% on imported EVs. The coalition's letter said such policies are why the U.S. "is not grappling with a massive surge in cut-rate Chinese vehicles that are not only capable of collecting and transmitting personal data back to the Chinese government."

The letter represents a rare alignment between competing factions of the U.S. auto industry. It was signed by leaders of trade groups representing domestic and international car companies, auto dealers, suppliers and the EV industry.
